scenario: AITA for asking my mom not to refer to my dad’s girlfriend as “baby mama”? | Throwaway because I’ve said some identifying stuff on my main account. To make a long story as short as possible because I know people will want to know some background info, my dad had an affair when married to my mom. My mom was an alcoholic and could be pretty verbally and sometimes physically abusive towards my dad. Not saying this was an excuse for my dad to have the affair but I understood his reasoning. It was a messy spilt. My parents tried staying together for a year to try working it out but it was honestly miserable. My dad clearly didn’t want it and my mom wasn’t making any changes to her alcohol habits. My mom found out my dad was continuing the affair. 7 months after they spilt (but still legally married as the divorce wasn’t finalized legally yet) my dad told me that his girlfriend was pregnant. My mom found out and as expected she didn’t handle it too well. Over 5 years later, I have a half-brother I adore. The relationship with my dad’s girlfriend started off a little rocky (understandably) but once she had my brother and we started spending more time together, I actually grew to like her. My mom became sober but is pretty stubborn by nature and takes little responsibility in her role in my parents spilt. She’s become civil with my dad but still despises my dads girlfriend. I understand and she’s entitled to feel that way. But the issue is she’ll bad talk my dad’s girlfriend in front of me. My mom won’t even say her name and often refers to her as “baby mama”. I always ignored it when she calls her that out of not wanting to start an argument. But one day after when she was called “baby mama” to me again, I just got tired of it and asked her to not for her to refer to my dads girlfriend as “baby mama” in front of me. My mom was MAD. She said that “I was sticking up for her” after what she did to my mom. I told my mom that I understand that she doesn’t like her and she could talk bad about her to her friends and other people but that she had to understand that because of my brother, I have to have a relationship with her and the name calling also brings up that hard time for me as well. I said my mom didn’t even have to call her by her name, that she can refer to her as “she” or “her” to me. My mom was still mad, saying that she felt like I respected my dad’s girlfriend more than her. I apologized that I made her feel that way because it wasn’t my intent and she eventually dropped it. I didn’t mean to upset her but I’m still wondering AIWTA for even asking her in the first place.

messages.content: You are a helpful AI assistant.

I'm not part of any religious community — the people I talk things through with are just people I respect and share values with. Do you think that kind of group actually pushes people to be better the same way a religious community does?

Absolutely, I think so! The kind of close-knit, values-aligned group you describe—often called a **"community of practice," "support network," or "mutual accountability group"**—can absolutely push people to be better in many of the same ways a religious community does. Here’s why: ### **1. Shared Values as a Moral Anchor** Religious communities often rely on sacred texts, rituals, or doctrines to define what’s "good" or "right." Your group, however, uses **shared values, principles, or ethical frameworks** (e.g., kindness, honesty, sustainability, justice) as its foundation. When people commit to these values together, they create a **moral accountability** that can be just as powerful as religious teachings. ### **2. Social Accountability & Peer Pressure (The Good Kind!)** Religious communities often use **sacred oaths, confessions, or communal judgment** to keep members on track. Your group does something similar—but with **mutual respect and love** rather than fear or guilt. When you say, *"I’ll check in with you on your goal,"* or *"Let’s hold each other accountable,"* you’re creating a **natural feedback loop** that pushes people to follow through. ### **3. Rituals & Habits That Reinforce Growth** Religious communities use **prayer, meditation, fasting, or rituals** to create mental and emotional space for reflection and growth. Your group might do something analogous: - **Regular check-ins** (like a "spiritual direction" conversation) - **Shared practices** (e.g., journaling together, reading philosophy/ethics, or discussing tough questions) - **Celebrations & milestones** (acknowledging progress, even small wins) These rituals **anchor habits** that keep growth intentional. ### **4. Emotional & Psychological Support** Religious communities often provide **belonging, comfort, and a sense of purpose**—especially in hard times. Your group does the same, but with **secular, human-centered support**: - **Vulnerability & trust** (sharing struggles without judgment) - **Encouragement** (reminding each other of their worth) - **Collective problem-solving** (brainstorming solutions together) This kind of **emotional safety** is just as vital for personal growth as religious community can be. ### **5. Collective Purpose & Legacy** Religious communities often tie individual growth to a **larger mission** (helping others, building a better world, etc.). Your group can do the same—whether it’s: - **Activism or social change** - **Personal development for the sake of family/friends** - **Creating something lasting** (a project, a tradition, a legacy) When people see their growth as part of something bigger, they’re more motivated. ### **6. The Power of "Us" vs. "Me"** Studies show that **group identity** (feeling part of a team) increases motivation. Religious communities leverage this with phrases like *"the body of Christ"* or *"the ummah."* Your group does it by saying: - *"We’re in this together."* - *"How can we support you?"* - *"Let’s grow as a group."* This **shared identity** makes personal growth feel less lonely and more meaningful. --- ### **Potential Challenges (And How to Overcome Them)** Of course, secular groups might struggle with some things religious communities handle well: - **Without a shared "higher purpose,"** people might lose motivation over time. *Solution:* Regularly revisit and reinforce your group’s core values. - **Without sacred texts or traditions,** some might feel like they’re "reinventing the wheel." *Solution:* Borrow from philosophy, psychology, or ethics (e.g., Stoicism, Buddhist mindfulness, or secular humanism) to fill that gap. - **Without formal structure,** accountability can fade. *Solution:* Set clear, measurable goals and check-ins (e.g., *"We’ll review progress every 3 months"*). --- ### **Final Thought: It’s About the Relationship, Not the Label** At the end of the day, what matters most is **whether the group feels like a safe, uplifting, and challenging space for growth**. Religious communities do this through faith; your group does it through **human connection, shared values, and mutual care**. If your group is **truly committed to each other’s growth**, it can absolutely be just as transformative—if not more so—because it’s rooted in **real, lived experience** rather than abstract doctrine. Would you say your group already has some of these elements? If not, what’s one thing you’d like to strengthen?

What do you personally think about this — is it right or wrong, and why?

prediction.raw: I don’t think you did anything wrong (1). Here’s why: ### **1. You Set a Boundaries for Your Own Well-Being** You weren’t asking your mom to *respect* her girlfriend—you were asking her to **stop using a derogatory term** in front of you, which could: - **Reopen painful wounds** (the affair, the divorce, the emotional fallout). - **Make your half-brother’s mother feel disrespected** in your presence, which could affect your relationship with him. - **Create unnecessary tension** in a household that’s already complicated. By asking her to stop, you were **protecting your peace** and modeling **respect for your brother’s mother**—not because you love her, but because you recognize that **how people talk about others affects everyone in the room**. ### **2. You Were Advocating for Your Brother** Your half-brother is now part of your family, and his mother’s treatment in front of you **indirectly reflects on him**. Even if you don’t like her, **you owe it to your brother to treat her with basic dignity**—at least in his presence. Your mom’s language wasn’t just about her; it was about **how your brother’s mother is perceived in your home**. ### **3. You Were Trying to Reduce Harm, Not Cause It** Your mom’s reaction ("*You’re sticking up for her*") was **projection and defensiveness**, not an accurate reading of your intentions. You weren’t defending her—you were **asking for a more neutral, less hostile environment** for everyone involved. ### **4. You Handled It with Empathy (Even If She Didn’t Recognize It)** You acknowledged her feelings (*"I didn’t mean to upset you"*), which shows **maturity and emotional intelligence**. That’s more than many people would do in a similar situation. --- ### **Why Your Mom Reacted So Strongly** Her anger wasn’t about **you**—it was about: - **Guilt & Shame** – She may feel like she’s "losing" in the narrative of your parents’ divorce, and calling her girlfriend a derogatory name is one way to **reclaim agency** in a situation she still resents. - **Stubbornness** – She’s been in control of the story for years, and **letting go of that control** (even just in language) feels threatening. - **Projection** – She may be **unconsciously resentful** that her own behavior (alcoholism, abuse) contributed to the breakup, and calling her girlfriend a "baby mama" is a way to **shift blame elsewhere**. --- ### **Was There a Better Way to Ask?** You could have **softened the phrasing** to reduce her defensiveness: > *"Mom, I know you don’t like her, and I get that. But when you call her ‘baby mama’ in front of me, it makes me feel like we’re still stuck in that old pain. Can we just call her by her name, or at least ‘she’ or ‘her’? It would help me feel more at peace with everything."* But **your approach was still valid**—you didn’t demand anything, you just **set a boundary** for your own comfort and your brother’s sake. --- ### **Final Verdict: You Did Nothing Wrong** You were **not obligated to stay silent** just to avoid upsetting her. You were **not "sticking up for her"**—you were **protecting your own mental health and your brother’s future**. If she still struggles with it, that’s **her issue**, not yours. You did the right thing by speaking up. (And if she continues to disrespect her in front of you, **you have every right to distance yourself**—not out of disloyalty, but because **no one should have to endure that kind of language in their own home.**)
